docs.title: FluxRules
docs.text: FluxRules is a lightweight Python library for defining and managing business rules. It evaluates rules against facts using a fast, deterministic engine inspired by Drools’ Phreak algorithm.

docs.title: Core Capabilities
docs.text:
• Create Rules
  • Validate the rules
  • Evaluate a ruleset against facts using the top-level Python API.
  • Run rule evaluation through FluxRules’ Phreak engine in stateless or streaming mode.
  • Retrieve evaluation explanations.
  • Use optional HTTP endpoints for evaluation, validation, explanations, and health checks.

docs.title: Advanced Capabilities
docs.text:
• Build stateful and streaming evaluation flows.
  • Load simple or nested rules directly from YAML files.
  • Register and execute custom action handlers.
  • Normalize heterogeneous facts using loader and pipeline stages.
  • Model nested facts and cross-fact joins.

See Usage: Advanced Capabilities for runnable example mapping.

docs.title: Project Scope
docs.text:
This repository currently focuses on:

  • In-process Python library usage.
  • Optional API layer and integrations through extras.
  • Developer-facing examples and tests.

This repository does not include a hosted control plane.

The package source is in src/fluxrules, and examples are in examples/.

docs.title: Action Registry
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Custom Actions.

Advanced patterns for registering and managing custom actions.

docs.title: Basic registry operations
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.plugins.actions import action_registry

# List all registered actions
all_actions = action_registry.list_actions()
print(f"Registered actions: {all_actions}")

# Filter actions by category
notifications = action_registry.get_actions_by_category("notifications")

docs.title: Action metadata
docs.text:
Every registered action exposes metadata:

# python skip
from fluxrules.plugins.actions import action_registry, action

@action(
    name="send_alert",
    description="Send alert to monitoring system",
    category="alerts"
)
def send_alert(**kwargs):
    return {"sent": True}

# Access metadata (after registration)
all_actions = action_registry.list_actions()
print(f"Registered actions: {all_actions}")

docs.title: Direct execution
docs.text:
# python skip
# Demonstration of action registry API
result = action_registry.execute(
    "send_alert",
    severity="high",
    message="Fraud detected"
)

docs.title: Batch execution
docs.text:
# python skip
# Batch execution of actions
actions = ["send_alert", "log_event", "notify_team"]
for action_name in actions:
    result = action_registry.execute(action_name, **kwargs)

docs.title: Algorithm Fidelity: PHREAK vs the Reference Evaluator
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The FluxRules Engine.

FluxRules ships one production engine (PHREAK). To guard against defects in shared code, the test suite checks PHREAK against an independent, dependency-free reference evaluator (fluxrules.services.reference_evaluator.ReferenceEvaluator). Because the two implementations share no matching code, agreeing on results is strong evidence of correctness.

docs.title: Verification approach
docs.text:
Test dataset: cross_border_payment_risk_triage (3 facts, shared use case)

Test rules: All 31 example rules with varying complexity:

  • Simple conditions (1 field)
  • Complex AND/OR logic
  • NOT operators
  • Nested groups

Verification method:

  1. Load the same ruleset into PHREAK and the reference evaluator
  2. Evaluate identical facts
  3. Compare fired_rules and actions
  4. Assert complete parity

The same harness also compares PHREAK's stateless and streaming modes to confirm a fact fires the same rules on first sight in either mode.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
✅ COMPLETE PARITY - PHREAK matches the reference evaluator on all test cases.

Test Case PHREAK Reference Match Simple condition ✅ ✅ ✅ AND groups ✅ ✅ ✅ OR groups ✅ ✅ ✅ NOT operator ✅ ✅ ✅ Nested groups ✅ ✅ ✅ Multiple rules ✅ ✅ ✅

Conclusion: PHREAK's optimized matching is semantically equivalent to the naive reference evaluator across the supported condition surface.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts.

FluxRules is a lightweight rule evaluation engine with a clean layered architecture. This page describes the system design from the condition tree down to engine execution.

docs.title: Evaluation Flow: From Fact to Result
Single Fact Evaluation (Simple API)
docs.text:
User: engine.evaluate({"amount": 5000, "country": "NG"})
  │
  ├─→ [1. Validate fact structure]
  │
  ├─→ [2. Iterate loaded rules]
  │    (via the PHREAK network)
  │
  ├─→ [3. For each rule:
  │       - Evaluate conditions against fact
  │       - If matched: add to fired_rules list
  │       - If matched & action exists: execute action
  │
  ├─→ [4. Collect results]
  │    - fired_rules: List[int] (matched rule IDs)
  │    - actions: List[Any] (action results)
  │    - latency_ms: float (execution time)
  │
  └─→ EvaluationResult(fired_rules=[1, 3], actions=["flag"], latency_ms=0.45)

docs.title: Multi-Step Workflow (Session-Based)
docs.text:
User: session = service.create_session()
  │
  ├─→ [1. Add facts incrementally]
  │    session.add_fact("user_type", "premium")
  │    session.add_fact("amount", 10000)
  │
  ├─→ [2. Evaluate against accumulated facts]
  │    result = session.evaluate()
  │
  ├─→ [3. Session remembers state (optional)]
  │    - Save snapshot for recovery
  │    - Restore in another process
  │
  └─→ EvaluationResult (same structure as simple API)

docs.title: The Engine: PHREAK
docs.text: For evaluation modes and selection guidance, see The FluxRules Engine and Choosing an Evaluation Mode.

docs.title: PHREAK (Phased Evaluation and Knowledge-the single engine)
docs.text:
Data flow: 

Load rules → [Store rules list]
              ↓
Fact input → [Linear iteration over rules]
              ├→ For each rule: evaluate condition
              ├→ Match? Add to results
              ↓
          [Produce EvaluationResult]
          ↓
          [Discard working memory for next fact]

Stateless mode (default):

  • Most HTTP/stateless workloads

  • Rules added/removed frequently

  • Low memory footprint required

  • Single-fact evaluation (typical)

docs.title: Streaming mode (opt-in)
docs.text:
Data flow: 

Load rules → [Build PHREAK network]
              ↓
Fact input → [Assert into working memory]
              ├→ Match new/changed facts
              └→ Report fired delta
              ↓
          [Produce EvaluationResult]
          ↓
          [Working memory persists across calls]

When to use:

  • Many facts over same rule set within a session
  • Event streams where only changes matter
  • Incremental fact updates (assert/retract)

docs.title: Condition Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
The conditions is a recursive JSON structure that's validated, compiled, and executed:

Input condition (F DSL or dict):
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["NG", "US"]))

Compiled condition tree:
{
  "type": "group",
  "op": "AND",
  "children": [
    {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "in", "value": ["NG", "US"]}
  ]
}
  │
  ├─→ [1. Parse & Validate]
  │    - Check syntax (type, op, field names)
  │    - Ensure operator is valid (==, !=, <, >, in, contains, etc.)
  │
  ├─→ [2. Convert to AST]
  │    - Build tree of condition nodes
  │    - Resolve operator functions
  │
  ├─→ [3. Evaluate against fact]
  │    - Traverse AST
  │    - Apply operators to fact values
  │    - Short-circuit AND/OR when possible
  │
  └─→ boolean result (True = rule fires)

docs.title: Data Model: Rule
docs.text:
# python skip
Rule(
    name="high_value_payment",           # Identifier
    domain="fraud_detection",             # Grouping
    tags=frozenset(["tier_1", "urgent"]), # Cross-cutting labels
    priority=10,                          # Execution order (higher first)
    conditions={...},                  # The condition tree above
    action="flag_for_review",             # Or callable
    persist=False                         # Optional: store in database
)

Key design:

  • Rule is immutable once created (frozen Pydantic model)
  • Conditions are pure predicates (no side effects)
  • Actions are simple strings or callables
  • Domain/tags allow flexible rule organization

docs.title: Pluggability Points
docs.text: FluxRules allows extension at three key layers:

docs.text:

class MyEngine(BaseEngine):
    def load_rules(self, rules: List[Rule]) -> None: ...
    def evaluate(self, fact: Dict) -> EvaluationResult: ...

docs.title: 2. Custom Actions
docs.text:
# python skip
@action(name="email_alert", category="notifications")
def email_alert(recipient: str, subject: str) -> bool:
    send_email(recipient, subject)
    return True

docs.text:
# python skip
class UpperCase(Transform):
    def apply(self, fact: Dict) -> Dict:
        return {k: v.upper() if isinstance(v, str) else v for k, v in fact.items()}

docs.title: Standalone (Single Process)
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────┐
│  Your Application    │
│  ├─ PhreakEngine     │
│  └─ Rules            │
└──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Evidence-first: All documentation backed by working code
  2. Pydantic v2: Rule validation via Pydantic (not home-grown)
  3. Pluggable: Custom engines, actions, transforms via simple interfaces
  4. Fast: Production-grade performance (ms-level latency)
  5. Simple: Minimal API surface, small learning curve
  6. Lazy by default: PHREAK's on-demand evaluation minimizes overhead

docs.title: Authoring Rules
docs.text:
A rule is a condition plus an action. The condition says when the rule fires. This page explains the ways to write that condition, which one to pick first, and why.

Short answer: write conditions with F expressions. Use a dictionary or YAML only when your rules come from outside your Python code.

docs.title: The same rule, four ways
docs.text:
All four forms below describe one rule: "fire when the amount is over 5000 and the country is US."

from fluxrules import F, Rule, RuleBuilder

# 1. F expression (first choice)
by_expression = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"),
    action="review",
)

# 2. RuleBuilder, step by step (it also takes an F expression)
by_builder = (
    RuleBuilder(1)
    .name("high_value_us")
    .condition((F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"))
    .action("review")
    .build()
)

# 3. Dictionary (the stored format)
by_dict = Rule(
    id=1,
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions={
        "type": "group",
        "op": "AND",
        "children": [
            {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
            {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"},
        ],
    },
    action="review",
)

# They are the same rule underneath.
assert by_expression.conditions == by_builder.conditions == by_dict.conditions

The fourth form is a YAML file, which holds the same dictionary:

- id: 1
  name: high_value_us
  action: review
  conditions:
    type: group
    op: AND
    children:
      - {type: condition, field: amount, op: ">", value: 5000}
      - {type: condition, field: country, op: "==", value: US}

docs.title: Which one should I use?
docs.text:
You are... Use Why Writing rules in Python code F expressions Shortest, reads like the rule, checked by your editor Building a rule step by step in code RuleBuilder Fields are set one at a time and checked as you go Loading rules from a database or an API Dictionary That is the format they are stored in Letting people edit rules without touching code YAML A plain file, no Python needed

If you are unsure, start with F. You can always print the dictionary behind an expression with .to_dict(), so nothing is hidden.

docs.title: Why F comes first
docs.text:
It reads like the rule. Compare the two:

(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

{"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [
    {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"}]}

Same meaning. The first is one line and the second is four. The shared example rule in examples/ has eight checks and two nested ORs. It is about 10 lines with F and about 70 as a dictionary, and the dictionary buries the logic in brackets.

It catches mistakes early. An editor can see that F("amount") > 5000 is Python. It cannot see that "op": ">" is an operator, so a typo such as "op": "=>" only shows up when the rule is built.

It costs nothing at run time. F is a thin layer over the dictionary. An expression turns into the same dictionary the engine always used, so stored rules, YAML files and the HTTP API do not change. There is no second engine and no slower path.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
F("amount") is a field reference. Python's comparison operators on it do not return True or False. They return a Condition object that holds a dictionary:

You write It builds F("x") > 5 {"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": ">", "value": 5} a & b {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a \| b {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} ~a {"type": "not", "condition": a} F("x").exists() {"type": "exists", "field": "x"}

Rule(conditions=...) and RuleBuilder.condition(...) accept a Condition or a dictionary, and a Condition is turned into its dictionary right away. After that point there is only one format.

One detail: a & b & c builds nested groups, (a & b) & c, while a dictionary you write by hand usually has one flat group of three. They give the same results. Only the shape differs.

docs.title: What to keep in mind
docs.text:
Wrap every comparison in parentheses. Python applies & and | before > and ==, so without parentheses the expression means something else and usually fails with a TypeError.

# python skip - the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")   # correct
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"       # wrong

Field names are exact. F("Amount") and F("amount") are different fields. If a fact has amount and a rule asks for Amount, FluxRules raises FieldNotFoundError and suggests the right name, instead of quietly never matching. A field that is simply not in the fact, with no similar key, returns False. That keeps rulesets that serve different kinds of facts working.

Use exists() for fields that may be missing. F("promo").exists() is true when the key is present and not None, and it never raises.

Pass a list to isin. Write F("country").isin(["NG", "GH"]), not F("country").isin("NG", "GH").

Match the type of the value to the type of the field. Comparing a number field to a string does not raise. It just never matches.

docs.title: Check a rule before you use it
docs.text:
There are three layers, from earliest to latest:

  1. When you build the Rule. An unknown operator, a missing key or a malformed tree raises ConditionValidationError immediately.
  2. Before you deploy. validate(rules) checks a whole list and returns a list of problems, empty when all is well. Run it in CI.
  3. While evaluating. FieldNotFoundError flags a field name that is a case variant of a key in the fact.
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow"),
]

assert validate(rules) == []

See Conditions for every operator and the full validation guide.

docs.title: Moving existing dictionary rules to F
docs.text:
You do not have to. Dictionaries keep working and can sit next to F rules in the same ruleset. When you do want to switch, the mapping is mechanical:

Dictionary F expression {"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": ">", "value": 5} F("x") > 5 "op": "in", "value": [...] F("x").isin([...]) "op": "contains" F("x").contains(v) {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a & b {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} a \| b {"type": "not", "condition": a} ~a {"type": "exists", "field": "x"} F("x").exists()

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The FluxRules Engine.

Performance characteristics of the FluxRules PHREAK engine.

docs.title: Evidence boundary
docs.text:
The repository has two benchmark categories:

  1. Pure matcher evidence - tests/performance/test_scale_readiness.py directly evaluated 1,000,000 generated facts against 1,200 generated rules on commit a572be9 using CPython 3.11.13 on macOS arm64. It compared 2,000 complete fired-rule sets against ReferenceEvaluator, measured 428.82 facts/s and 140.70 MB peak RSS, and passed the 150 facts/s and 2,048 MB thresholds. The retained artifact is .research/scale-readiness-2026-09-16.json.
  2. Boundary evidence - actions, persistence, HTTP serialization, auth, queueing, process concurrency, and sticky streaming are separate costs and contracts. They are not included in the pure matcher result above.

Do not interpret the pure matcher measurement as end-to-end service throughput. The next benchmark set should use the same deterministic rule/fact profiles and report exact result parity, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, peak RSS, and failure counts for each boundary independently.

docs.text:
• Python 3.11
  • Single-threaded evaluation
  • Test dataset: cross_border_payment_risk_triage (shared dataset, 3 facts)
  • Rules: 10-1000 typical rules

docs.text:
Rule Count PHREAK 10 rules ~0.5ms 100 rules ~2ms 500 rules ~10ms 1000 rules ~20ms

Notes: - Latency grows roughly linearly with rule count - Latency measured in EvaluationResult.latency_ms

docs.text:

Notes: - Constant footprint - rules are loaded once and facts evaluate independently

docs.text:
Rule Count Time 10 rules ~1ms 100 rules ~1ms 1000 rules ~2ms

Note: load_rules() cost is small; most work happens at evaluate() time.

  • PHREAK: ~2000 evaluations/sec (500 rules, simple conditions)

Note: Actual throughput depends on rule complexity and condition logic.

docs.title: Required follow-up profiles
docs.text:
Before making broader capacity claims, run and retain separate results for:

  • selective, dense/hot-field, nested, and high-match rule distributions;
  • deterministic no-op action execution and action failure handling;
  • persistence/load phases with result parity after reload;
  • in-process HTTP and a real local server path with JSON/error timing;
  • bounded queue producer/consumer behavior and backpressure;
  • one, two, and four process workers with ordered result parity;
  • sticky streaming shards with repeated/changed facts and memory growth.

Each profile must identify whether it measures matcher-only or end-to-end work.

docs.title: Choosing an Evaluation Mode
docs.text:
Prerequisites: The FluxRules Engine.

FluxRules ships a single engine (PHREAK), so there is no engine to pick. The one decision you make is which evaluation mode fits your workload.

docs.title: Decision flowchart
docs.text:
1. Do you keep state between facts?
  2. No - each request is independent → Stateless mode (default)

  3. Yes - you assert/retract into a long-lived session → Streaming mode

  4. What is the evaluation pattern?

  5. Request-response (HTTP) → Stateless mode
  6. Batch (many independent facts) → Stateless mode

  7. Event stream where only changes matter → Streaming mode

  8. Do you need per-fact deltas?

  9. No, you want the full fired set every call → Stateless mode
  10. Yes, you want only what changed since the last fact → Streaming mode

docs.title: Quick decision guide
docs.text: Scenario Mode HTTP API for fraud scoring Stateless Batch data pipeline Stateless Rules updated daily Stateless (reload rules) Single-file rule config Stateless Long-lived session with retractions Streaming Event stream, deltas only Streaming

docs.title: Default recommendation
docs.text:
Use stateless mode unless you specifically need persistent working memory:

  • Simplest deployment and reasoning (no state to manage)
  • Lowest memory footprint (nothing retained between calls)
  • Ideal for request-response and batch workloads

Enable streaming only when you need incremental deltas across a session.

docs.title: Complex Conditions
docs.text:
Combine multiple simple conditions using AND / OR / NOT logic.

Prerequisites: Authoring Rules and Conditions & Operators - covers all operators and the three authoring formats.

docs.title: AND Logic
docs.text:
All conditions must be true for the rule to fire.

from fluxrules import F, Rule, PhreakEngine

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_international",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").not_in(["US", "CA", "GB"])),
    action="manual_review",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "country": "NG"}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "country": "NG"}).fired_rules)   # []

Dict equivalent (the wire format stored in YAML/DB):

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "not_in", "value": ["US", "CA", "GB"]},
    ],
}

docs.title: OR Logic
docs.text:
At least one condition must be true.

rule = Rule(
    name="risky_pattern",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 5000)
        | (F("velocity_1h") >= 5)
        | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 80)
    ),
    action="block_payment",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 6000, "velocity_1h": 1, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 1000, "velocity_1h": 6, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 1000, "velocity_1h": 1, "ip_risk_score": 30}).fired_rules)   # []

docs.title: NOT Logic
docs.text:
The condition must be false.

rule = Rule(
    name="unverified_high_value",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.com"))
    ),
    action="step_up_auth",
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "email_domain": "gmail.com"}).fired_rules)    # [1]
print(engine.evaluate({"amount": 3000, "email_domain": "trusted.com"}).fired_rules)  # []

docs.title: Nested Logic
docs.text:
Combine AND, OR, and NOT for multi-part rules:

rule = Rule(
    name="payment_risk_triage",
    conditions=(
        # 1. Large amount
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        # 2. High-risk country OR high IP risk
        & (
            (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70)
        )
        # 3. New or unverified device/account
        & (
            (F("account_age_days") < 7)
            | (F("device_age_days") < 7)
        )
        # 4. NOT a trusted email domain
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
    ),
    action="manual_review",
)

The F DSL reads as close to the logic description as you can get in Python. The same tree in dict form grows by about 4× in line count, which is why the F DSL is the recommended authoring format.

docs.title: Operator precedence
docs.text:
Python's & and | bind more tightly than >, <, ==. Always wrap each individual leaf in parentheses before composing:

# python skip - the Wrong line deliberately raises to show the trap
# Correct - each leaf is parenthesised
(F("amount") > 2000) & (F("country") == "NG")

# Wrong - & binds before ==, raising a TypeError
F("amount") > 2000 & F("country") == "NG"

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: This page introduces the fundamental concepts you need to work with FluxRules. All code references are to src/fluxrules/.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
A Rule is the core abstraction. It combines a condition, an action, and metadata for organization.

Source: src/fluxrules/domain/unified_rule.py

from fluxrules import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="payment_risk_high",
    conditions={
        "type": "condition",
        "field": "amount",
        "op": ">",
        "value": 5000,
    },
    action="manual_review",
    domain="fraud_detection",
    tags=frozenset(["tier_0", "high_value"]),
    priority=100,
)

Key Attributes:

  • id - Auto-generated unique identifier (or manual override)

  • name - Human-readable rule name

  • domain - Logical grouping (e.g., "fraud_detection", "compliance")

  • tags - String set for filtering and categorization

  • conditions - Nested tree defining when the rule fires

  • action - What to do when the rule matches

  • priority - Execution order (higher = runs first). All matching rules fire; priority only orders them. Ties are currently broken by rule ID (highest first), which is not a guaranteed contract, so use distinct priorities if order matters. Same-group, same-priority rules raise a validation warning.

See: examples/18_unified_rule.py

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
An Engine evaluates facts against loaded rules and returns matched rules and actions.

Source: src/fluxrules/engine/ (interfaces and implementations)

A single engine is available:

  • PhreakEngine (the only engine) - Lazy, agenda-driven evaluation with stateless (default) and streaming modes

Quick Example: 

from fluxrules import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

fact = {"amount": 6000, "country": "NG"}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)

For evaluation modes, see The FluxRules Engine. For mode selection guidance, see Choosing an Evaluation Mode.

docs.title: Fact
docs.text:
A Fact is a JSON-like dictionary representing data to evaluate against rules.

Structure: Flat or nested dictionaries Example: 

fact = {
    "fact_id": "txn-001",
    "amount": 2500.00,
    "currency": "USD",
    "country": "NG",
    "ip_risk_score": 85,
    "velocity_1h": 3,
    "account_age_days": 7,
}

Important: A fact is stateless by default. Each engine.evaluate(fact) call is independent.

See: examples/06_working_memory.py (state management patterns)

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
A condition tree is a nested tree that defines when a rule fires. It combines:

  • Simple conditions (field comparisons)

  • Logical operators (AND, OR, NOT)

  • Nested groups

Basic condition: 

from fluxrules import F

F("amount") > 5000

Nested conditions (with AND/OR): & means both must be true, | means either one is enough. 

from fluxrules import F

(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"]))

With NOT: ~ means the condition must be false. 

from fluxrules import F

~F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.com")

Every expression is stored as a plain dictionary tree, the same format YAML files and the HTTP API use. The AND example above is stored as:

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "in", "value": ["NG", "SN"]},
    ],
}

You can write the dictionary by hand when you prefer. See Authoring Rules for all the ways to write a condition.

Validation: Use from fluxrules.domain.conditions.validation import validate_conditions

See: examples/02_complex_conditions.py, examples/13_complex_rules.py

docs.title: Evaluation Result
docs.text:
When you evaluate a fact, the engine returns a result object with:

result = engine.evaluate(fact)

# result.fired_rules - list of rule IDs that matched
# result.actions - list of actions to execute
# result.latency_ms - execution time in milliseconds

Example: 

print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")  # [1001, 1003]
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")       # ['manual_review', 'block_payment']
print(f"Time: {result.latency_ms}ms")     # 1.2ms

See: examples/15_action_system.py

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
A Domain is a logical grouping of rules. Rules with the same domain typically handle a specific problem area.

For example depending on how your rules are grouped you can give a name e.g. compliance or fraud_detections etc.

Filtering by domain: 

from fluxrules import F, PhreakEngine, Rule

# Define rules with domains
rule1 = Rule(name="rule1", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag")
rule2 = Rule(name="rule2", domain="compliance", conditions=F("country") == "NG", action="review")
rule3 = Rule(name="rule3", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("type") == "transaction", action="process")

all_rules = [rule1, rule2, rule3]

# Load only fraud_detection rules
fraud_rules = [r for r in all_rules if r.domain == "fraud_detection"]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(fraud_rules)

See: examples/03_domains_and_tags.py

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
A Tag is a string label for categorization and filtering.

Filtering by tag: 

# Get all tier_0 rules
tier0_rules = [r for r in all_rules if "tier_0" in (r.tags or set())]

See: examples/03_domains_and_tags.py

docs.title: Shared Evaluation Dataset
docs.text:
To learn FluxRules, all examples use a shared cross_border_payment_risk_triage dataset:

# python skip
from shared_use_case import SHARED_FACTS, USE_CASE_NAME, build_shared_rules

# 3 test transactions
for fact in SHARED_FACTS:
    print(fact["fact_id"])  # txn-001, txn-002, txn-003

# 3 payment-risk rules
rules = build_shared_rules()

# 8-condition nested tree
dsl = complex_risk_condition()

This shared context lets you focus on learning features without context-switching between problem domains.

docs.title: Conditions & Rule Authoring
docs.text:
A rule's conditions field defines when the rule fires. FluxRules gives you three ways to author conditions, the same condition tree on the wire for all three, and a set of tools to validate before you deploy.

Start with Authoring Rules for how to choose between them. This page is the reference: every operator and every validation tool.

docs.title: 1. F DSL - recommended for Python code
docs.text:
Write conditions as natural Python expressions using the F helper. Each expression compiles to a condition dict the engine accepts; you never touch raw dicts.

from fluxrules import F, Rule

# Single leaf
rule = Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="review",
)

# AND - both must hold
rule = Rule(
    name="high_value_us",
    conditions=(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"),
    action="review",
)

# OR - either suffices
rule = Rule(
    name="risky_origin",
    conditions=(F("country").isin(["NG", "SN"])) | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70),
    action="block",
)

# NOT
rule = Rule(
    name="unverified",
    conditions=~F("verified").exists(),
    action="step_up",
)

# Composed
rule = Rule(
    name="fraud_triage",
    conditions=(
        (F("amount") > 2000)
        & (F("payment_method").isin(["crypto", "prepaid_card"]))
        & (
            (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            | (F("ip_risk_score") >= 70)
        )
        & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
    ),
    action="manual_review",
)

Operator precedence warning - Python's & and | bind more tightly than comparisons like >, <, ==. Always wrap each individual condition in parentheses:

# python skip - the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
# Correct
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

# Wrong - & binds before ==, raising a TypeError at runtime
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"

docs.title: 2. Dict / YAML - for config-driven rules
docs.text:
The dict format is the wire and storage format. Use it when rules come from a database, YAML file, or API response.

Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions={"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
    action="review",
)

YAML (loaded with load_rules_from_yaml, see YAML Rules):

name: high_value
conditions:
  type: condition
  field: amount
  op: ">"
  value: 5000
action: review

AND/OR in dict form:

{
    "type": "group",
    "op": "AND",
    "children": [
        {"type": "condition", "field": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 5000},
        {"type": "condition", "field": "country", "op": "==", "value": "US"},
    ],
}

The F DSL and the dict format describe the same conditions. Mix them freely: a Rule built with F(...) stores a dictionary tree like one built from a dict, and loads back from YAML the same way. One difference in shape: a & b & c nests as (a & b) & c, where a hand-written dict usually has one flat group of three. Both give the same results.

docs.title: 3. RuleBuilder - fluent step-by-step construction
docs.text:
RuleBuilder chains method calls and validates each step. Useful when building rules programmatically where you want to catch errors early.

from fluxrules import F, RuleBuilder

rule = (
    RuleBuilder()
    .name("high_value_us")
    .priority(10)
    .condition((F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US"))
    .action("review")
    .build()
)

.condition() accepts both an F expression and a raw dict.

docs.title: Comparison (Python dunders)
docs.text:
F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x") == v "==" or "eq" Equal F("x") != v "!=" or "ne" Not equal F("x") > v ">" or "gt" Greater than F("x") >= v ">=" or "gte" Greater than or equal F("x") < v "<" or "lt" Less than F("x") <= v "<=" or "lte" Less than or equal

The six comparison operators also accept their word-form aliases in dict/YAML (eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte), normalised before evaluation.

docs.title: Collection membership
docs.text: F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").isin(["a", "b"]) "in" Value is a member of the list F("x").not_in(["a"]) "not_in" Value is not a member

docs.title: String / collection containment
docs.text: F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").contains("tag") "contains" Collection or string contains value F("x").not_contains("flag") "not_contains" Does not contain

docs.title: String matching
docs.text:
Both sides are coerced to strings before matching.

F expression Dict "op" Meaning F("x").starts_with("adm") "starts_with" str(x).startswith(...) F("x").ends_with(".com") "ends_with" str(x).endswith(...) F("x").regex("^4[0-9]{12}") "regex" re.search(pattern, str(x)) - matches anywhere in the string, so add ^ to anchor at the start

docs.title: Boolean composition (F DSL)
docs.text: Operator Meaning Dict equivalent a & b AND {"type": "group", "op": "AND", "children": [a, b]} a \| b OR {"type": "group", "op": "OR", "children": [a, b]} ~a NOT {"type": "not", "condition": a}

docs.title: Field presence
docs.text:
F("email").exists()          # True when "email" key is in facts and not None
~F("email").exists()         # True when "email" is absent or None

Dict equivalent:

{"type": "exists", "field": "email"}

Use exists() when a field might legitimately be absent - condition nodes raise FieldNotFoundError if the field is a case variant of a present key (e.g. Amount vs amount). exists() never raises.

docs.title: What to keep in mind when authoring rules
Field names are exact and case-sensitive
docs.text:
F("Amount") and F("amount") are different fields. If a fact arrives with {"amount": 5000} and the condition says F("Amount"), the rule raises a FieldNotFoundError because the field is a case variant of a present key. For genuinely different schemas (multi-domain rulesets), absent fields that are not a case variant of any present key return False silently, which is the correct behaviour.

# Fact: {"amount": 5000}
F("Amount") > 1000   # raises FieldNotFoundError - did you mean 'amount'?
F("amount") > 1000   # evaluates correctly

docs.title: Operator precedence: always use parentheses
docs.text:
Python evaluates & and | before >, <, ==. The rule is simple: wrap every individual F(...) comparison in its own parentheses before composing:

# python skip - the unsafe line deliberately raises to show the trap
# safe - each leaf is wrapped
(F("amount") > 5000) & (F("country") == "US")

# unsafe - raises TypeError
F("amount") > 5000 & F("country") == "US"

docs.title: Use exists() for optional fields
docs.text:
A condition node on a field that is absent raises (if the name looks like a typo) or returns False (if genuinely different schema). When a field is intentionally optional, guard it with exists():

# Only fires if "promo_code" is present AND matches
F("promo_code").exists() & (F("promo_code") == "SUMMER24")

docs.title: Value types must match
docs.text:
A numeric field compared with a string will not raise, but will silently not match. Match the value type to the field type:

F("amount") > 5000      # number field → number value
F("status") == "active" # string field → string value
F("tags").contains("vip")  # list field → scalar value to find in it

docs.title: isin takes a list, not positional args
docs.text:
# python skip - the second line deliberately raises to show the trap
F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"])   # correct
F("country").isin("NG", "SN", "GH")    # wrong - TypeError

docs.title: Combining AND chains cleanly
docs.text:
For long AND chains, align the & operators at the start of each line:

conditions=(
    (F("amount") > 2000)
    & (F("payment_method").isin(["crypto", "prepaid_card"]))
    & (F("chargeback_ratio") >= 0.1)
    & ~(F("email_domain").ends_with("trusted.example"))
),

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: FluxRules validates condition trees at rule construction time (Pydantic) and exposes an explicit validate step for bulk checks before deployment.

docs.title: Automatic validation at construction
docs.text:
Invalid conditions are caught when you build the Rule:

# python skip - this block deliberately raises to show the validation error
from fluxrules import F, Rule

Rule(
    name="bad",
    conditions={"type": "condition", "field": "x", "op": "???", "value": 1},
    action="flag",
)
# raises ConditionValidationError: unknown operator '???'

Missing required keys, unknown operators, and malformed tree shapes all raise ConditionValidationError immediately.

docs.title: validate() - check a batch without evaluating
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="allow"),
]

issues = validate(rules)
if issues:
    for issue in issues:
        print(issue)
else:
    print("All rules valid")

validate() returns a list of human-readable strings - empty means all rules passed. Use it in CI before deploying a new ruleset.

docs.title: FieldNotFoundError at evaluation time
docs.text:
When a condition field is absent from the incoming fact and the name is a case variant of a present key (e.g. Amount vs amount), the engine raises instead of silently returning False:

from fluxrules import F, FieldNotFoundError, Rule, evaluate

rule = Rule(name="r", conditions=F("Amount") > 5000, action="flag")
try:
    evaluate(rule, {"amount": 6000})
except FieldNotFoundError as e:
    print(e)
# Field 'Amount' not found in fact. Did you mean 'amount'? Available keys: ['amount']

To deliberately test whether a field is present before comparing its value, use F("field").exists():

# Does not raise even when "score" is absent
F("score").exists() & (F("score") >= 90)

docs.title: Full validation example
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule, validate

rules = [
    Rule(
        name="fraud_check",
        conditions=(
            (F("amount") > 10000)
            & (F("country").isin(["NG", "SN", "GH"]))
            & ~(F("verified").exists())
        ),
        action="block",
        priority=10,
    ),
    Rule(
        name="vip_fast_track",
        conditions=(F("tier") == "gold") | (F("spend_ytd") >= 50000),
        action="expedite",
        priority=5,
    ),
]

issues = validate(rules)
assert issues == [], issues

from fluxrules import evaluate

fact = {"amount": 15000, "country": "NG"}
result = evaluate(rules, fact)
print(result.fired_rules)   # rule ids that matched
print(result.actions)       # ["block"]

docs.title: Condition tree reference
docs.text:
The dict / YAML format uses these node shapes:

Node type Required keys Optional keys condition type, field, op, value - group / and / or type, children (or conditions) op (default AND) not type, condition - exists type, field -

Accepted aliases: "and", "or", "not", "exists", "group", "composite".

docs.title: Cross-Fact Rules
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Working Memory (fact storage).

Correlate multiple facts with cross-fact logic.

docs.title: Single-fact limitation
docs.text:
Standard engines evaluate one fact at a time:

from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
result1 = engine.evaluate({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 5000})
result2 = engine.evaluate({"customer_id": "c2", "amount": 1000})
# No correlation between result1 and result2

docs.title: Pattern 1: Pre-aggregate upstream
docs.text:
Combine facts before evaluation:

# Combine multiple facts before rule evaluation
combined = {
    "transaction_1_amount": 5000,
    "transaction_2_amount": 3000,
    "total_24h": 8000,  # Pre-computed
    "customer_id": "c1"
}

result = engine.evaluate(combined)

docs.title: Pattern 2: Multi-step with sessions
docs.text:
Use sessions to accumulate state:

# python skip
from fluxrules.services.rule_service import RuleService

service = RuleService.create()
session = service.create_session()

# Step 1: Check first condition
session.add_fact("transaction_1", {"amount": 5000})
result1 = session.evaluate()

# Step 2: Add second condition
session.add_fact("transaction_2", {"amount": 3000})
result2 = session.evaluate()

# Both facts now in session state

docs.title: Pattern 3: Working memory
docs.text:
Assert multiple facts and query them:

# Store facts in working memory
id1 = engine.assert_fact({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 5000})
id2 = engine.assert_fact({"customer_id": "c1", "amount": 3000})

# Evaluate combined logic
result = engine.evaluate({
    "customer_id": "c1",
    "total": 8000,  # Computed from stored facts
})

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Multiple related facts → Aggregate and pass combined dict
  • Multi-step workflow → Use sessions with fact accumulation
  • Temporal correlation → Store facts in working memory

docs.title: Custom Actions
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Rule, action field) and Validation Framework.

Actions are strings or tuples of strings that are executed when a rule fires. FluxRules supports:

  1. String actions - Simple action names from your application
  2. Action registry - Register custom handlers with the @action decorator
  3. Built-in actions - Default actions like flag and alert

docs.title: Using actions in rules
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rule1 = Rule(
    name="check_high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="require_approval",  # Single action (string)
    persist=False,
)

rule2 = Rule(
    name="check_fraud",
    conditions=F("ip_risk_score") > 80,
    actions=("block", "notify_security"),  # Multiple actions (tuple)
    persist=False,
)

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule1, rule2])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 7500, "ip_risk_score": 90})
print(f"Actions: {result.actions}")  # ["require_approval"] + ["block", "notify_security"]

docs.title: Built-in actions
docs.text:
• flag - Mark fact for manual review
  • alert - Send alert notification
  • skip - Skip further evaluation
  • Custom strings - Any string your application recognizes

docs.title: Register custom action handlers
docs.text:
Use the @action decorator to register a handler that executes when an action fires:

from fluxrules.plugins.actions import action
from fluxrules.plugins.actions import action_registry


# Register a simple action
@action(
    name="send_approval_request",
    description="Send approval request to team",
    category="notifications",
)
def send_approval_request(transaction_id: str, amount: int) -> dict:
    """Execute when 'send_approval_request' action fires."""

    # Your implementation: call API, send email, etc.
    print(f"Sending approval request for txn {transaction_id} ({amount})")

    return {"success": True, "action": "send_approval_request", "transaction_id": transaction_id}


# Register an async action
@action(
    name="log_to_database",
    description="Log event to database",
    category="logging",
    async_handler=True,
)
async def log_to_database(event_id: str) -> dict:
    """Async action handler."""

    # Your async implementation
    return {"logged": True, "event_id": event_id}


# List all registered actions

docs.title: Custom Engines
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Concepts (Engine) and Features.

FluxRules provides one standard engine: PhreakEngine (lazy, agenda-driven). You can implement a custom engine by subclassing BaseEngine.

docs.title: Why custom engines?
docs.text:
• Specialized algorithms - Implement domain-specific matching logic
  • Performance optimization - Tailor to your data patterns
  • Integration - Wrap external rule systems

docs.title: Custom engine structure
docs.text:
from fluxrules.engine import BaseEngine
from fluxrules.domain import Rule
from fluxrules.domain.conditions.evaluator import evaluate_conditions
from typing import Any


class MyCustomEngine(BaseEngine):
    """Custom rule evaluation engine."""

    def _evaluate_rules(
        self, rule_ids: list[int], facts: dict[str, Any]
    ) -> tuple[list[int], list[str], dict[int, str]]:
        """Evaluate discovered rules and return fired IDs, actions, explanations."""
        fired_ids = []
        actions = []
        explanations = {}
        for rule_id in rule_ids:
            rule = self.rule_repository.get(rule_id)
            if rule and evaluate_conditions(rule.conditions, facts):
                fired_ids.append(rule_id)
                actions.extend(rule.actions)
                explanations[rule_id] = f"Rule {rule.name} matched"
        return fired_ids, actions, explanations

docs.text:
from fluxrules import F

rule = Rule(
    name="high_value",
    conditions=F("amount") > 1000,
    action="review",
    persist=False,
)
engine = MyCustomEngine()
engine.load_rules([rule])

result = engine.evaluate({"amount": 5000, "country": "US"})
print(f"Matched: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Your Question Answered: Custom Transforms in FactPipeline
docs.text: This document directly answers your question about what happens when you want to pass your own transformation function or class instead of built-in transforms like Flatten().

docs.title: Your Question
docs.text: In this example from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten, Rename, FieldType, Defaults, Require... what happen if a user want to pass his own transformation function or class instead of Flatten(). How can FactPipeline accept these or what happens if all custom functions or class needed to be passed within FactPipeline.

docs.title: 1. Plain Functions Don't Work
docs.text:
# python skip
# ❌ This will FAIL
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline


def my_flatten(fact):
    return {k.replace("_", "."): v for k, v in fact.items()}


normalize = FactPipeline([my_flatten])
# → AttributeError: 'function' object has no attribute 'metadata'

Why? FactPipeline expects all transforms to have a .metadata property, which only exists on Transform classes.

docs.title: 2. Plain Classes Don't Work
docs.text:
# python skip
# ❌ This will FAIL
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline


class MyFlatten:
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return {k.replace("_", "."): v for k, v in fact.items()}


normalize = FactPipeline([MyFlatten()])
# → AttributeError: 'MyFlatten' object has no attribute 'metadata'

Why? Same reason-they don't inherit from Transform and don't have .metadata.

docs.title: 3. Classes Inheriting from Transform Work Perfectly
docs.text:
# ✅ This WORKS
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline, Flatten, Require, Transform, TransformMetadata


class MyFlatten(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return {k.replace("_", "."): v for k, v in fact.items()}

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(name="MyFlatten")


normalize = FactPipeline([MyFlatten()])  # ✓ Works!

Why? Because your class now: - Inherits from Transform - Implements __call__ (makes it callable) - Implements metadata property (publishes transform contract)

docs.title: 4. FactPipeline is Designed to Accept Custom Classes
docs.text:
The framework is designed to let you write your own transforms. Built-in transforms like Flatten(), Rename(), etc. are just examples-they're all Transform subclasses too!

# All of these are Transform subclasses
from fluxrules.pipeline import Flatten, Rename

Flatten()  # ← Built-in
Rename({"user_id": ["user.id"]})  # ← Built-in
MyFlatten()  # ← Your class (same pattern!)

docs.title: The Complete Pattern
docs.text:
Here's what your custom transform needs to be accepted by FactPipeline:

from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform, TransformMetadata
from typing import Any


class YourTransform(Transform):
    """Your transform description."""

    # 1. Define __init__ if you need configuration
    def __init__(self, config_param: str) -> None:
        self.config_param = config_param

    # 2. Implement __call__ to transform facts
    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        # Process the fact
        out = dict(fact)  # Always create a copy!
        # ... your transformation logic ...
        return out

    # 3. Implement metadata property
    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="YourTransform",  # Required
            version="1.0.0",  # Recommended
            required_input_fields=["field"],  # Optional but good to have
            output_fields=["output_field"],  # Optional but good to have
            errors_raised=[ValueError],  # Optional but important for error handling
            description="What it does",  # Optional but helpful
        )

That's it! Now you can use it in your pipeline:

pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),
        YourTransform(config_param="value"),  # ← Your custom transform
        Require(["field"]),
    ]
)

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Field Validation
docs.text:
class ValidateEmail(Transform):
    """Validate email format."""

    def __init__(self, field: str = "email"):
        self.field = field

    def __call__(self, fact):
        email = fact.get(self.field)
        if not email or "@" not in email:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid email: {email}")
        return fact  # Pass through if valid

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="ValidateEmail",
            required_input_fields=[self.field],
            errors_raised=[ValueError],
        )


# Use it
pipeline = FactPipeline([ValidateEmail(), Require(["email"])])

docs.title: Example 2: Enrichment with External Data
docs.text:
class EnrichCountry(Transform):
    """Look up country details from a database."""

    def __init__(self, db: dict):
        self.db = db

    def __call__(self, fact):
        code = fact.get("country_code")
        if not code or code not in self.db:
            raise KeyError(f"Unknown country: {code}")

        details = self.db[code]
        out = dict(fact)
        out["country_name"] = details["name"]
        out["region"] = details["region"]
        return out

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="EnrichCountry",
            required_input_fields=["country_code"],
            output_fields=["country_name", "region"],
            errors_raised=[KeyError],
        )


# Use it
countries = {
    "US": {"name": "United States", "region": "Americas"},
    "NG": {"name": "Nigeria", "region": "Africa"},
}

pipeline = FactPipeline([EnrichCountry(db=countries), Require(["country_name"])])

docs.title: Example 3: Complex Data Transformation
docs.text:
class NormalizePhoneNumber(Transform):
    """Normalize phone numbers to a standard format."""

    def __init__(self, field: str = "phone", country_code: str = "US"):
        self.field = field
        self.country_code = country_code

    def __call__(self, fact):
        phone = fact.get(self.field)
        if not phone:
            return fact  # Skip if missing

        # Remove non-digits
        digits = "".join(c for c in str(phone) if c.isdigit())

        if self.country_code == "US" and len(digits) == 10:
            # Format as (XXX) XXX-XXXX
            normalized = f"({digits[:3]}) {digits[3:6]}-{digits[6:]}"
        else:
            normalized = digits

        out = dict(fact)
        out[self.field] = normalized
        return out

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="NormalizePhoneNumber",
            required_input_fields=[self.field],
            output_fields=[self.field],
        )


# Use it
pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        NormalizePhoneNumber(field="phone", country_code="US"),
        ValidateEmail(),
    ]
)

docs.title: What About Serialization?
docs.text:
If you want to save your pipeline to YAML/JSON and load it back, your transform needs to_dict() and from_dict():

class MyTransform(Transform):
    def __init__(self, field: str):
        self.field = field

    def __call__(self, fact):
        # ... implementation ...
        return fact

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(name="MyTransform", required_input_fields=[self.field])

    # Add these two methods for serialization
    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {"type": "MyTransform", "field": self.field}

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, spec: dict[str, Any]) -> "MyTransform":
        return cls(field=spec["field"])


# Register it so FactPipeline can find it
from fluxrules.pipeline import register

register(MyTransform)

# Now serialization works
pipeline = FactPipeline([MyTransform(field="email")])
spec = pipeline.to_dict()  # Serialize to dict
restored = FactPipeline.from_dict(spec)  # Deserialize from dict

docs.title: How FactPipeline Works (Under the Hood)
docs.text:
When you create a pipeline, FactPipeline checks each item:

# python skip
normalize = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),  # Is this a Transform? ✓ Yes → Use it
        MyTransform(field="email"),  # Is this a Transform? ✓ Yes → Use it
        "invalid",  # Is this a Transform? ✗ No → Error!
        plain_function,  # Is this a Transform? ✗ No → Error!
    ]
)

The check is: isinstance(thing, Transform)

That's why: - ✅ All Transform subclasses work (built-in or custom) - ❌ Plain functions fail - ❌ Plain classes fail (unless they inherit from Transform) - ❌ Strings fail - ❌ Generic callables fail

docs.title: Pitfall 1: Forgetting the metadata Property
docs.text:
# python skip
# ❌ Wrong: AttributeError on execution
class MyTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return fact

    # Missing: @property metadata


# ✅ Right: Always provide metadata
class MyTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return fact

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(name="MyTransform")

docs.title: Pitfall 2: Mutating the Input Fact
docs.text:
# ❌ Wrong: Causes hard-to-debug issues with retries/error policies
class BadTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        fact["new_field"] = "value"  # MUTATES INPUT!
        return fact


# ✅ Right: Always create a copy
class GoodTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        out = dict(fact)  # Create copy FIRST
        out["new_field"] = "value"
        return out

docs.title: Pitfall 3: Not Handling Missing Fields
docs.text:
# ❌ Wrong: Crashes if field is missing
class BadTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return {**fact, "upper": fact["name"].upper()}  # KeyError if no "name"


# ✅ Right: Check for field existence
class GoodTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        if "name" not in fact:
            return fact  # Or raise ValueError to trigger error policy
        out = dict(fact)
        out["upper"] = fact["name"].upper()
        return out

docs.title: Pitfall 4: Over-wrapping Transforms in FactPipeline
docs.text:
Transforms compose directly with >> and | - no need to wrap each one in its own FactPipeline first.

# python skip
my_transform = MyClass()  # inherits from Transform
another = AnotherClass()  # inherits from Transform

# ✅ Right: Chain transforms directly
pipeline = my_transform >> another

# ✅ Also fine: pass them as a list
pipeline = FactPipeline([my_transform, another])

# 😕 Unnecessary: works, but verbose
pipeline = FactPipeline([my_transform]) >> FactPipeline([another])

>> only works when both sides inherit from Transform (or are FactPipelines). A plain function or bare class doesn't define >> and will raise TypeError - the fix is to make it a Transform subclass, not to wrap it in a FactPipeline.

docs.title: When to Create a Custom Transform
docs.text: Scenario Do This Apply a simple function to a field Use MapValues(fn, fields=[...]) Validate data Create a Transform that raises ValueError Enrich from external data Create a stateful Transform with a database connection Complex multi-step logic Compose multiple transforms with >> and Conditional Serialize to YAML Implement to_dict() and from_dict()

docs.title: Complete Working Example
docs.text:
Here's a complete, production-ready example combining everything:

from fluxrules.pipeline import (
    FactPipeline,
    Flatten,
    Require,
    Transform,
    TransformMetadata,
    ErrorPolicy,
    ErrorAction,
    FactLoader,
    IterableSource,
)
from typing import Any


# Your custom transforms
class ValidateEmail(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        email = fact.get("email", "")
        if "@" not in email:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid email: {email}")
        return fact

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="ValidateEmail",
            required_input_fields=["email"],
            errors_raised=[ValueError],
        )


class Uppercase(Transform):
    def __init__(self, fields):
        self.fields = fields

    def __call__(self, fact):
        out = dict(fact)
        for field in self.fields:
            if isinstance(out.get(field), str):
                out[field] = out[field].upper()
        return out

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="Uppercase",
            required_input_fields=self.fields,
            output_fields=self.fields,
        )


# Create pipeline with custom transforms
pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),
        Uppercase(fields=["country"]),
        ValidateEmail(),
        Require(["email", "user_id"]),
    ],
    name="normalize",
    error_policy=ErrorPolicy(
        default=ErrorAction.FAIL,
        routes={ValueError: ErrorAction.SKIP},
    ),
)

# Process data
facts = [
    {"user": {"id": "u1"}, "email": "alice@example.com", "country": "us"},
    {"user": {"id": "u2"}, "email": "invalid", "country": "uk"},  # Invalid → skip
    {"user": {"id": "u3"}, "email": "bob@example.com", "country": "ng"},
]

loader = FactLoader(IterableSource(facts), pipeline, on_error="collect")

print("Processed facts:")
for fact in loader:
    print(f"  {fact}")

print(f"\nSkipped: {len(loader.dead_letter)} records")
for dead in loader.dead_letter:
    print(f"  {dead['error']}: {dead['data']}")

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
✅ You CAN create your own transforms - Inherit from Transform - Implement __call__ and metadata - Use them in FactPipeline just like built-in transforms

❌ You CANNOT use plain functions or generic classes - FactPipeline requires isinstance(thing, Transform) to be True - Anything else will raise AttributeError: 'object' has no attribute 'metadata'

🎯 Best practices - Always copy facts before modifying: out = dict(fact) - Always implement metadata property - Raise ValueError for validation errors, KeyError for transient failures - Test transforms in isolation with pytest

# python skip
# ❌ THIS WON'T WORK - Plain function
def my_flatten(fact):

normalize = FactPipeline(

    def __call__(self, fact):

from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform, TransformMetadata

docs.title: Three Ways to Add Custom Logic
Way 1: Custom Transform Class (Recommended)
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform, TransformMetadata


class Uppercase(Transform):
    def __init__(self, fields):
        self.fields = fields

    def __call__(self, fact):
        out = dict(fact)
        for field in self.fields:
            if isinstance(out.get(field), str):
                out[field] = out[field].upper()
        return out

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="Uppercase",
            required_input_fields=self.fields,
            output_fields=self.fields,
        )


# Use it
pipeline = FactPipeline([Uppercase(fields=["name", "country"])])

Pros: - Full IDE support and type checking - Supports serialization (YAML/JSON) - Publishable metadata for introspection - Works with error policies and hooks - Unit testable in isolation

Cons: - More boilerplate than a plain function

docs.title: Way 2: Use MapValues for Simple Cases
docs.text:
If you just want to apply a function to certain fields:

from fluxrules.pipeline import MapValues

# Instead of creating a custom class for simple cases:
pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        MapValues(str.upper, fields=["name", "country"]),
        MapValues(int, fields=["amount"]),
    ]
)

Pros: - No custom class needed - Built-in error handling - Simple and declarative

Cons: - Limited to field-level transformations

docs.title: Way 3: Composition with Conditional
docs.text:
For branching logic, use composition instead of conditionals inside transforms:

from fluxrules.pipeline import Conditional


# DON'T: Put branching inside a transform
class BadApproach(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        if fact.get("source") == "legacy":
            ...  # handle legacy
        else:
            ...  # handle modern
        # ... complex nested logic ...


# DO: Use Conditional composition
legacy_transform = FactPipeline([Rename({"id": ["legacy_id"]})])
modern_transform = FactPipeline([Rename({"id": ["modern_id"]})])

pipeline = Conditional(
    predicate=lambda f: f.get("source") == "legacy",
    then_transform=legacy_transform,
    else_transform=modern_transform,
)

docs.title: How FactPipeline Validates Transforms
docs.text:
When you pass something to FactPipeline([...]), it checks:

# python skip
# Illustrative sketch of FactPipeline's internal dispatch, not runnable code.
class FactPipeline:
    def _eval(self, node, fact):
        # First check: Is this a Transform?
        if isinstance(node, Transform):  # ← This is where it fails for functions/plain classes
            return self._run_transform(node, fact)

        if isinstance(node, CompositionNode):  # ← Or a composition operator result
            ...  # handle composition

So FactPipeline only accepts things that isinstance(..., Transform) returns True for.

docs.title: Mistake 1: Forgetting metadata property
docs.text:
# python skip
# ❌ WRONG
class MyTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return fact

    # Missing @property metadata


# Run it
pipeline = FactPipeline([MyTransform()])
# AttributeError: 'MyTransform' object has no attribute 'metadata'


# ✅ CORRECT
class MyTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        return fact

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(name="MyTransform")


pipeline = FactPipeline([MyTransform()])  # Works!

docs.title: Mistake 2: Mutating the input fact
docs.text:
# ❌ WRONG: Modifies the input
class BadTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        fact["new_field"] = "value"  # ← Mutates input!
        return fact


# This causes issues with retries and error policies
# because the original fact is already modified


# ✅ CORRECT: Create a copy
class GoodTransform(Transform):
    def __call__(self, fact):
        out = dict(fact)  # ← Create a copy
        out["new_field"] = "value"
        return out

docs.title: Mistake 3: Over-wrapping transforms in FactPipeline
docs.text:
Transforms compose directly with >> and |. You do not need to wrap each one in its own FactPipeline first.

# python skip
transform_a = MyClass()
transform_b = MyClass()

# ✅ CORRECT: Chain transforms directly
pipeline = transform_a >> transform_b

# ✅ ALSO CORRECT: Pass them as a list
pipeline = FactPipeline([transform_a, transform_b])

# 😕 UNNECESSARY: Works, but verbose - no need to wrap each transform
pipeline = FactPipeline([transform_a]) >> FactPipeline([transform_b])

Note: transform_a and transform_b must still inherit from Transform. Plain functions and bare classes don't define >>, so they raise TypeError. The operators are provided by the Transform base class.

docs.title: Decision Tree
docs.text:
"I want to add custom logic to my pipeline..."

  ├─ "It's just a simple function to call on one field"
  │  └─→ Use MapValues(fn, fields=[...])
  │
  ├─ "I need branching/conditional logic"
  │  └─→ Use Conditional(...) with composition operators
  │
  ├─ "I need validation or error handling"
  │  └─→ Create a Transform that raises ValueError
  │
  ├─ "I need to serialize to YAML/JSON later"
  │  └─→ Create a Transform with to_dict/from_dict
  │
  └─ "I need something more complex"
     └─→ Create a Transform class with __call__ and metadata

docs.title: Real-World Example from Your Question
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import (
    FactPipeline,
    Flatten,
    Rename,
    FieldType,
    Defaults,
    Require,
    Transform,
    TransformMetadata,
)

# Your original normalize pipeline
normalize = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),  # nested -> dot notation
        Rename({"user_id": ["user.id", "userId"]}),  # first alias wins
        FieldType({"amount": float}),  # type coercion
        Defaults({"country": "US"}),  # fill missing fields
        Require(["user_id", "amount"]),  # fail-fast validation
    ],
    name="normalize",
)

fact = normalize({"user": {"id": "u_1"}, "amount": "1500"})
# Output: {'user.id': 'u_1', 'user_id': 'u_1', 'amount': 1500.0, 'country': 'US'}


# Now add a custom transform to the pipeline
class LogTransform(Transform):
    """Log each fact being processed."""

    def __init__(self, prefix="Processing"):
        self.prefix = prefix

    def __call__(self, fact):
        print(f"{self.prefix}: {fact}")
        return fact  # Pass through unchanged

    @property
    def metadata(self):
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="LogTransform", description=f"Log facts with prefix: {self.prefix}"
        )


# Add it to your pipeline
enhanced_normalize = FactPipeline(
    [
        Flatten(),
        Rename({"user_id": ["user.id", "userId"]}),
        LogTransform(prefix="After rename"),  # ← Your custom transform
        FieldType({"amount": float}),
        LogTransform(prefix="After coercion"),  # ← Another custom transform
        Defaults({"country": "US"}),
        Require(["user_id", "amount"]),
    ],
    name="enhanced_normalize",
)

fact = enhanced_normalize({"user": {"id": "u_1"}, "amount": "1500"})
# Output:
# After rename: {'user.id': 'u_1', 'user_id': 'u_1', 'amount': '1500'}
# After coercion: {'user.id': 'u_1', 'user_id': 'u_1', 'amount': 1500.0, 'country': 'US'}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The key rule: All transforms in FactPipeline must inherit from Transform.

  • Can't pass: Plain functions, generic classes, bare callables
  • Must pass: Classes that inherit from Transform and implement __call__ + metadata

For detailed patterns and examples, see: - Custom Transforms Guide - Comprehensive patterns and best practices - Example 29: Custom Transforms - Real-world working examples - FactPipeline Documentation - Full framework overview

docs.title: Custom Transforms
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Fact Pipeline (Transform basics).

Create custom transforms for domain-specific fact enrichment and validation.

docs.title: Custom transform structure
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform, TransformMetadata
from typing import Any


class MyTransform(Transform):
    """Custom transform for fact enrichment."""

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="my_transform",
            description="My custom transform",
            output_fields=["enriched_field"],
        )

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Transform the fact."""
        # Your custom logic
        fact["enriched_field"] = "value"
        return fact

docs.title: Example: Geographic enrichment
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import Transform, TransformMetadata
import json


class GeoEnricher(Transform):
    """Enrich facts with geographic data."""

    def __init__(self, geo_db: dict[str, dict[str, Any]]):
        self.geo_db = geo_db

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(
            name="geo_enricher",
            description="Add geographic risk scores",
            required_input_fields=["country"],
            output_fields=["geo_risk_score", "geo_region"],
        )

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        country = fact.get("country")
        if country and country in self.geo_db:
            enriched = dict(fact)
            enriched["geo_risk_score"] = self.geo_db[country]["risk"]
            enriched["geo_region"] = self.geo_db[country]["region"]
            return enriched
        return dict(fact)

docs.title: Using custom transforms
docs.text:
from fluxrules.pipeline import FactPipeline

pipeline = FactPipeline(
    [
        GeoEnricher({"NG": {"risk": 8, "region": "Africa"}}),
    ],
    name="enrich_geo",
)

fact = {"country": "NG", "amount": 5000}
enriched = pipeline(fact)
# enriched has geo_risk_score and geo_region added

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
class ValidatingTransform(Transform):
    """Validate and transform."""

    def __call__(self, fact: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        if "required_field" not in fact:
            raise ValueError("Missing required_field")

        # Transform
        processed = dict(fact)
        processed["processed"] = True
        return processed

    @property
    def metadata(self) -> TransformMetadata:
        return TransformMetadata(name="validating_transform")


# Pipeline propagates errors
try:
    bad_fact = {"amount": 5000}
    pipeline(bad_fact)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Transform failed: {e}")

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Combine custom transforms in pipelines:

enricher = GeoEnricher({"NG": {"risk": 8, "region": "Africa"}})
validator = ValidatingTransform()

# Sequence: enrich then validate
pipeline = enricher >> validator

raw_fact = {"country": "NG", "amount": 5000, "required_field": True}
fact = pipeline(raw_fact)

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
Prerequisites: All Concepts.

High-level flowchart for FluxRules usage decisions.

docs.title: Is FluxRules right for your use case?
docs.text:
Do you need to:

  • Execute business rules conditionally? (Yes → continue)
  • Match complex logic against data? (Yes → continue)
  • Change rules without code deployment? (Yes → continue)

If all yes: FluxRules is a good fit.

docs.title: Integration: Library vs API?
docs.text:
Library mode (in-process):

  • Import FluxRules in your app
  • Evaluate locally
  • No network overhead
  • Single deployment unit
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

engine = PhreakEngine()
rule = Rule(
    name="adult",
    conditions=F("age") >= 18,
    action="allow",
    persist=False,
)
engine.load_rules([rule])
fact = {"age": 21}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)

API mode (microservice):

  • Run FluxRules as separate service
  • Evaluate via HTTP
  • Network latency added
  • Separate deployment and scaling
curl -X POST http://fluxrules-service/api/v1/evaluate \
  -d '{"facts": {...}}'

Decision:

  • Single app, fast iteration → Library
  • Multiple services, shared rules → API
  • High scale requirements → API

docs.title: Persistence: Store rules or keep in-memory?
docs.text:
In-memory (default):

  • Rules defined in code
  • No database needed
  • Rules reset on app restart
# python skip
engine.load_rules([rule1, rule2, ...])

Persistent (database):

  • Rules stored in database
  • Load rules on startup
  • Audit trail available
  • Requires [sql] extra
export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...
service.persist_rules([rule1, rule2, ...])

Decision:

  • Prototype/testing → In-memory
  • Production/stable rules → Persistent
  • Rules change frequently → Persistent

docs.title: State management: Stateless or stateful?
docs.text:
Stateless (each evaluation independent):

  • Default behavior
  • No side effects between evaluations
  • Simple, predictable
# python skip
result1 = engine.evaluate(fact1)
result2 = engine.evaluate(fact2)  # No state from result1

Stateful (multi-step workflow with sessions):

  • Accumulate facts across evaluations
  • Session snapshot support
  • Requires [sql] extra
# python skip
session.add_fact("step1", value)
session.evaluate()
session.add_fact("step2", value)
session.evaluate()

Decision:

  • Single fact evaluation → Stateless
  • Multi-step workflow → Stateful

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Prerequisites: Custom Actions and Custom Engines.

FluxRules is designed for manual dependency injection via constructor parameters.

docs.title: Pattern
docs.text:
# python skip
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

# Inject dependencies
logger = get_logger("fluxrules")
metrics = get_metrics_collector()
database = get_database_connection()

# Pass to engine
engine = PhreakEngine(metrics_collector=metrics, logger=logger)


# Or to action
@action(name="log_and_store")
def log_and_store(database=database, logger=logger, **kwargs):
    logger.info(f"Storing: {kwargs}")
    database.insert(kwargs)
    return {"stored": True}

docs.title: No framework dependency
docs.text:
FluxRules has zero framework dependencies. Integrate with your existing DI setup:

# python skip
# FastAPI
from fastapi import Depends


@app.post("/evaluate")
def evaluate(request: Request, engine: Engine = Depends(get_engine)):
    return engine.evaluate(request.facts)


# Django
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404


def evaluate_view(request):
    engine = get_engine()  # From your service layer
    return engine.evaluate(request.POST)

docs.title: ServiceFactory and persistence
docs.text:
When you register a persistence adapter via ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter(), Rule(persist=True) and Rule.save() automatically delegate to that adapter rather than the built-in SQLite default. This is the recommended pattern for production deployments that use PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or another provider:

# python skip - requires a live database and session provider
from fluxrules.di import ServiceFactory
from fluxrules.config import RuntimeConfig, PersistenceConfig

ServiceFactory.create_persistence_adapter(
    session_provider=SessionLocal,          # your SQLAlchemy sessionmaker
    config=RuntimeConfig(
        persistence=PersistenceConfig(backend="postgres")
    ),
)

See Persistence for a full example.

docs.title: Domains and Tags
docs.text:
Organize and filter rules using domains (logical grouping) and tags (multi-dimensional labeling).

Prerequisites: Familiarity with Rules and rule creation (see Getting Started).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As your rule systems grow, you need ways to: - Organize rules by business area (fraud, compliance, marketing) - Filter rules at evaluation time (only evaluate tier_1 rules) - Manage rules by team or feature - Query rules without loading everything

Domains and tags enable this organization:

  • Domain: Single category each rule belongs to (mutually exclusive)
  • Tags: Multiple labels per rule (cross-cutting concerns)

docs.title: Domains
docs.text: A domain is a logical grouping. Each rule belongs to exactly one domain.

docs.title: Define a Domain
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="fraud_check",
    domain="fraud_detection",  # Single domain per rule
    conditions=F("amount") > 5000,
    action="flag_for_review"
)

Default domain is "default" if not specified:

from fluxrules import F

rule_no_domain = Rule(
    name="simple_rule",
    conditions=F("status") == "active",
    action="process"
)
# rule_no_domain.domain == "default"

docs.title: Query by Domain
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("status") == "active", action="flag"),
    Rule(name="r2", domain="compliance", conditions=F("country") == "US", action="block"),
    Rule(name="r3", domain="fraud_detection", conditions=F("amount") > 5000, action="review"),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Evaluate against a fact
fact = {"status": "active", "country": "US", "amount": 6000}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)
print(f"Fired rules: {result.fired_rules}")

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags are labels you add to rules for cross-cutting organization. A rule can have unlimited tags.

docs.title: Add Tags to a Rule
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F
from fluxrules.domain import Rule

rule = Rule(
    name="vip_fast_track",
    domain="marketing",
    tags=frozenset(["vip", "urgent", "auto_action"]),  # Multiple tags
    conditions=F("customer_tier") == "vip",
    action="fast_track_checkout"
)

Tags must be passed as frozenset[str]. Rule automatically converts lists to frozensets:

# python skip
# Both work:
# Rule(name="r1", conditions={...}, tags=frozenset(["tag1", "tag2"]))
# Rule(name="r2", conditions={...}, tags=["tag1", "tag2"])  # Converted to frozenset

docs.title: Query by Tags
docs.text:
from fluxrules import F, Rule
from fluxrules.engine.phreak import PhreakEngine

rules = [
    Rule(name="r1", tags=frozenset(["urgent", "vip"]), conditions=F("priority") == "high", action="action1"),
    Rule(name="r2", tags=frozenset(["low_priority"]), conditions=F("priority") == "low", action="action2"),
    Rule(name="r3", tags=frozenset(["urgent"]), conditions=F("type") == "alert", action="action3"),
]

engine = PhreakEngine()
engine.load_rules(rules)

# Evaluate against a fact
fact = {"priority": "high", "type": "notification"}
result = engine.evaluate(fact)
print(f"Fired: {result.fired_rules}")
